items.t: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after Trump says he pressed the board
items.s: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, a little more than a week after he resigned amid reports of extramarital affairs. Its shares jumped more than 33 percent on the news.
p: Nvidia’s board has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, reversing his resignation earlier this month. The chipmaker announced the move on Monday, and the company said the decision took effect immediately.

Huang stepped down after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman whom US intelligence is said to believe is a Chinese spy. Al Jazeera described the affairs as at least two in number and said the alleged spy was a suspected Chinese agent. Those claims are not confirmed in the sources.

President Donald Trump said on CNBC that he had spoken with the board “directly and indirectly” and had convinced its members to bring Huang back. He said the board had asked for assurances on national security risks and that his administration had provided them. Trump also said he had spoken with Huang on Sunday night, before the announcement.

Nvidia said its leadership had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk. Trump wrote on Truth Social that the government had no reason to believe the return posed any risk. The sources do not publish the assurances themselves, so their content can only be judged from these official statements.

The return followed a campaign by Elon Musk and others. A petition calling for Huang’s return drew more than 180,000 signatures within days of his departure, according to Al Jazeera. Musk posted that “the mistake has been corrected” after the announcement. Colette Kress, who had served as interim CEO, will remain chief financial officer.

Analysts said Huang’s role at Nvidia is central to the wider spending boom in data centres and chips. BBC News reported that the company sells chips to customers including Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, and has also provided funding to firms in its supply chain, a practice known as circular financing. Some investors worry that a pullback in Nvidia’s spending could spread to the wider US economy. Dan Ives said Nvidia could have lost as much as 30 percent of its value without Huang, a view Al Jazeera attributed to him.

Several issues remain open. Al Jazeera reported that investigations into the company by the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the Department of Justice are still ongoing. Goldman Sachs, cited by the BBC, expects investment in this spending wave to exceed $1 trillion in 2026. Early trading on Monday showed strong gains across major US indices, with the Nasdaq up 6.7 percent.
items.cav: The alleged spy link and the number of affairs are reported claims, not established facts, and the assurances given to the board have not been published. The sources also differ slightly on the share jump, with one saying more than 33 percent and another 33 percent.
items.op: A chipmaker’s leadership should not be settled by a president’s phone calls and national-security assurances the sources do not publish. Whatever the merits of Huang’s return, investors and citizens are being asked to trust private briefings while federal inquiries remain open. Transparency about what was promised, and to whom, should come before the market celebrates.

items.t: Trump backs Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as lawmakers press national security questions
items.s: US President Donald Trump has said he spoke with Nvidia’s board about Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive and that the company’s concerns over national security were addressed. House committees say the reinstatement “changes nothing” for their own inquiry.
p: Donald Trump told CNBC that he had spoken “directly and indirectly” with Nvidia’s board about the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, which he described as the correct decision. In a phone interview, Trump said he had also spoken with Huang the night before the board announced the move.

According to Trump, the board asked for assurances on national security risks, and the administration provided them. He said the government had conducted a “very thorough investigation” into Huang and concluded that Huang had shown bad judgement in somewhat unrelated incidents but had done nothing wrong. Trump said Huang had been exonerated. The evidence does not include the findings of that investigation, and Trump’s account is his own.
Trump also declined to say whether he had joined the Nvidia board meeting, saying only that he “was represented at the board”.

A spokesperson for the House intelligence committee told NBC News that the reinstatement changes nothing for three House committees, which plan a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on 1 December. Nvidia’s general counsel is due to appear the following day. The committee spokesperson said serious questions about national security implications still need answers.

Senator Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate intelligence committee, said the decision showed that national security was “up for sale”. Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Senate banking committee from January, called the decision “reckless” and said the board still owes Congress answers about the company’s compliance with US export controls.

The reinstatement follows reports, cited by the New York Times, that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had been in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 until this autumn. The Times reported this on the basis of people with knowledge of US intelligence reports, and the claims have not been confirmed in the evidence.

Markets responded strongly. Nvidia’s shares were reported to have risen by about 31 per cent at the start of trading, while the S&P 500 jumped 4.5 per cent. Reports on the size of the share gain vary, with one headline citing 33 per cent.
items.cav: The sources do not establish whether Huang was cleared of wrongdoing; that claim comes from Trump. The Alice Huang reports are second-hand, cited from the New York Times, which is behind a paywall. The share increase is reported inconsistently, as 31 per cent in one part of the coverage and 33 per cent in another.
items.op: A chief executive’s return matters to the public when it touches export controls and national security. When a president vouches for a company’s leader while Congress is still seeking answers, the public deserves the same transparency. The assurances given to the board should be disclosed, not left for closed-door sessions.

items.t: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he resigned
items.s: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, less than two weeks after he resigned. Its board said it had received input from senior US government levels before making the decision.
p: Nvidia’s board of directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, according to a company statement. The board said it was satisfied with “Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia” after a series of discussions and meetings.

The board said that, based on input from senior levels of the US government, it was confident Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk. It did not name the officials involved or describe the input in detail.
President Donald Trump praised Huang as a “great patriot and national treasure”. The Guardian’s live blog reported that Trump said he had spoken to the Nvidia board directly about Huang.

Colette Kress, who had served as interim CEO while keeping her role as chief financial officer, was thanked by the board for her service. The live blog’s headline said Nvidia shares rose 33% on the news, adding $1tn to the company’s value.
items.cav: The sources do not explain why Huang resigned. The government input is unnamed, and the 33% gain and $1tn figure appear only in the live-blog headline, so they are not confirmed in the excerpt.
items.op: A company’s leadership decision shaped by unnamed government input deserves more openness than a one-line assurance. Markets and the public should be told what officials said and why it satisfied the board. Without that, a national security clearance looks like a private deal.

items.t: Hacked Russian records point to more than 1,000 military suicides in the Ukraine war
items.s: Russian state records, obtained in leaked form and analysed by the Guardian, list more than a thousand soldiers as having taken their own lives since the invasion began. The newspaper and its sources believe the true total is higher.
p: The Guardian’s analysis of a cache of more than 11 million death certificates puts the number of Russian soldiers recorded as suicides since the full-scale invasion at over 1,000. The paper says that total roughly equals one regiment. The figures are drawn from records held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics body, which has not made them public.

The newspaper illustrates the pattern with one man, Alexei Bolgov, a sergeant guarding a headquarters in occupied Donetsk. In late 2024 he reportedly told his wife by phone that what he was witnessing was dreadful and promised to explain when he returned. According to a written account by his commander, which the Guardian has seen, he walked roughly 300 metres from his unit’s post into woodland about five weeks later and shot himself, shortly after his 29th birthday. “On the day of his death, Bolgov was in a withdrawn state,” the commander wrote.

A separate group of 885 deaths in or near Ukraine was logged as firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent”. Specialists warn that this label can hide suicides, and the Guardian says it independently confirmed several such cases as suicides. Taken together with the confirmed suicides, the paper counts 1,038 similar deaths, 885 of them in or near Ukraine.

Of the 1,087 suicides the paper has identified, at least 614 occurred in occupied Ukrainian territory or in the Russian border regions of Belgorod and Bryansk, while 113 entries give no location. More than half involved firearms, often near the front, at camps, training grounds and private homes. The wartime cases include 43 soldiers aged 18 or 19. The wider set also contains 108 men under 25 who died by suicide elsewhere in Russia, some of whom may have been conscripts pressed into contracts.

Recorded cases rose from more than 50 in 2022 to more than 200 in 2024, reaching a peak of 365 in 2025. The database already holds almost 300 suicides for 2026, which the paper describes as the second-highest yearly total of the war so far. It stresses that the records are incomplete and lag behind events at the front.

Analysts cited by the Guardian point to pressure from commanders and fellow soldiers, dread of lethal assignments, and contracts that offer little or no way out. Rob Lee of the Foreign Policy Research Institute described coercion by the military, including abuse and torture, and said it was unsurprising that some men take their own lives. Ivan Chuvilyaev, a spokesperson for Idite Lesom, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert, called the official count an underestimate: “I would say it is a low estimate.” He also argued that many self-inflicted deaths on the battlefield are probably logged as combat losses.

The Kremlin does not publish military suicide data and treats casualty figures as a state secret. The Guardian also examined the case of Sergei Savenok, a lieutenant colonel from the Irkutsk region who was found shot dead in occupied Luhansk in July 2023. Officials told his wife that he had died by suicide, yet he does not appear in the Rosstat suicide records. A certificate matching his date of birth instead records an injury from a handheld firearm of undetermined intent.
items.cav: The figures come from a hacked cache of death certificates and the Guardian’s own analysis, not from an official Russian publication, and the sources provided do not include a Kremlin response. The claims that the true number is higher are estimates from experts and activists, not measured totals, and the case details rely on a commander’s account and a wife’s report.
items.op: When a state hides its war dead, families and the public are left to rely on leaks and hacked files. Counting how soldiers die is basic accountability, not wartime propaganda. Until Moscow publishes its records, its silence should be read as a choice, and it deserves to be challenged.

items.t: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive just 11 days after he resigned
items.s: Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, 11 days after he stepped down amid reports of two extra-marital affairs. The chipmaker sits at the centre of the US-China race for technology leadership.
p: For a long time Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, was widely admired in the technology industry. His reputation shifted after allegations of two affairs emerged, one involving a businesswoman whom US officials allege is a Chinese intelligence asset. Those reports rattled the tech sector and global stock markets, and Huang resigned.

The first reports appeared on 29 October in the New York Times, which said Huang had been in a relationship with a businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is not related to him. US officials allege that she is linked to Singapore-based firm Megaspeed. Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife and has apologised for hurting his family.

A second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who has worked at the company for 18 years, prompted a board meeting. The board then announced that Huang was stepping down.

Within days a campaign called Bring Jensen Back was launched. It was reportedly started by current and former employees, partners, shareholders and supporters. Huang said he would be honoured to return if the board asked him. The board has now done so, saying his return was in the best interests of its stockholders, employees, partners and customers.

Huang's importance goes beyond his personal story. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips used to power the rapid growth of new technology over the past three years. Its customers include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Tesla. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company, according to the BBC.

Huang has also built close ties with political leaders. He has been courted by US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping. At a recent summit at the White House he was chosen from a group of 42 to stand beside the president, alongside Elon Musk.

Huang's personal fortune has also moved sharply. According to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, it reached close to $200bn earlier this year before falling to around $105bn. Born in Taiwan in 1963, he moved with his family to the US west coast as a child, studied electrical engineering and later founded Nvidia. He has long presented himself as a family man, and his two children now hold senior roles at the company.
Stephen Witt, author of a biography of Huang, told the BBC that Huang is a visionary and a demanding boss. Witt also said Huang shows a level of arrogance and self-deception.
items.cav: The affair allegations and the spy claim rest on New York Times reporting and on US officials who have not been named in the evidence, so the national security element is second-hand. The board has given only a brief reason for reversing course, and the evidence does not show what it reviewed before doing so.
items.op: A chief executive's private conduct is not automatically a matter for regulators, but a board that reverses itself within days owes shareholders a clear account. If a national security allegation was weighed, the public should be told how. Otherwise, a fan campaign has overridden the governance it is supposed to protect.

items.t: Thousands evacuated from Manchester Don Toliver concert after unknown substance released
items.s: Around 12,000 people were evacuated from a Don Toliver concert at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena after an unidentified irritant was reported in the crowd, police said. Dozens were treated by medics.
p: Police in Manchester, in northwest England, said on Monday that a Sunday-night show by the US rapper Don Toliver was emptied after people in the audience reported ill effects. Greater Manchester Police treated the situation as a major incident.

Attendance figures differ between outlets. Euronews put the crowd near 12,000 at the Co-op Live arena. A separate international report said more than 80 people had received treatment from medics, while the regional ambulance service said it had assessed over 50 people on site, some with eye and breathing problems.

Police said several people were treated on site and one was sent to hospital. Steph Parker of Greater Manchester Police said investigators were working out what the substance was. The venue said it was cooperating with officers to establish the source of the problem.

The ambulance service said decontamination took place at the venue. Toliver, an American singer who has worked with Travis Scott and Justin Bieber, is on the second leg of his Nitrous world tour and had been due to perform in London on Monday.
Reports on the number of people affected vary, and the sources available so far do not identify the substance.
items.cav: The sources do not say what the substance was, and the figures for people treated or assessed differ between the international report and the police and ambulance accounts. The story is described as developing, so details may change.
items.op: Audiences moved out of a packed arena are owed a clear account of what they were exposed to and whether the response was proportionate. The venue and police should publish their findings, not just reassurances, because public trust depends on it.

items.t: EU unveils 22nd Russia sanctions package, reviving ban on Russian ex-combatants entering the bloc
items.s: Ursula von der Leyen has presented a 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, covering banking, energy and sports. Unanimous approval from all 27 member states is still required.
p: Doubts had grown over whether the EU could agree meaningful new Russia sanctions at all. The European Commission is now trying to tighten the screws again, and von der Leyen has brought back a plan to keep Russian soldiers out of EU territory.

The package, presented as the 22nd round of measures over the war in Ukraine, also targets Russian banks, energy flows and sporting competitions. Each area is described in the Commission’s announcement, though the live coverage the reporting draws on offers only a summary of its contents.

The earlier 21st package was hard fought in July. A sanction on the transfer of liquefied natural gas was weakened, and a proposal to bar former combatants from the bloc was put off after France and Italy objected. Two oligarchs were then struck off the EU sanctions list in September.

That same month, von der Leyen argued in her annual address to the European Parliament that enforcing current measures mattered more than adding new ones. According to the reporting, the situation has since moved on: Moscow has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine, and several incidents in the EU have been blamed on Russia, among them a foiled attack on Leipzig airport.

Estonia has been the most vocal backer of barring Russian ex-combatants and of stopping athletes from competing under the Russian flag. Mark Rutte, speaking for Nato, stressed that Ukraine must keep receiving air defence systems and munitions.
The package is not assured of passage. It needs backing from every one of the 27 member states, yet the case that the EU has no need for fresh measures is becoming harder to make in Brussels.
items.cav: Blame for the Denmark assassination attempt, the Leipzig drone plot and the Black Sea strikes is attributed to Russia in the reporting, not confirmed by findings. The package’s details come from a live blog summary, and the final text may change in negotiations.
items.op: Sanctions only deserve trust if they are enforced and explained. Brussels should publish the legal basis and evidence behind each measure, and show how a ban on individuals will be applied fairly. Credibility, not announcements, will decide whether this package has any effect.

items.t: Nvidia shares surge as board brings back Jensen Huang as CEO, days after his resignation
items.s: Nvidia has restored Jensen Huang as chief executive less than two weeks after he stepped down over reports of extramarital affairs, one of them involving an alleged Chinese spy. The company's shares jumped sharply when trading opened in New York on Monday.
p: On Monday Nvidia said it had brought Huang back as president, chief executive and board member, with the change taking hold at once. The board voted unanimously after a series of meetings, and said its directors were satisfied with his “candor and ability to lead”.

The turnaround is abrupt. Only days earlier the board had said it would weigh internal and external candidates to succeed him, and its chair, Harvey Jones, told investors it had no plan to reinstate Huang. Huang had indicated he would return if the board asked him to.

Huang stepped down on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. At the time, US Attorney General Todd Blanche said the FBI was looking into reports that she had worked for the Chinese government, and that the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion. Beijing rejects the allegation.

Nvidia’s market value rose by more than $1 trillion as its shares climbed. Sources give different figures for the gain, between 30% and 33%, depending on when the price was measured. Wider markets also rallied, with the Nasdaq reported up between 5.9% and 6.5% in early trading. Micron, Intel and AMD also rose. The gains came after Nvidia shares fell close to 14% on Friday, a drop that followed a Reuters report, not confirmed by the BBC, that the US Securities and Exchange Commission was examining the company’s accounting.

Donald Trump, who had publicly urged the board to reappoint Huang, welcomed the move. He said the US government had no reason to think Huang’s return threatened national security, and pointed to Blanche’s statement that the government held no evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang.

Nvidia said senior US government officials had given input and that it was confident the return carried no national security risk. It also said an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation would continue. Huang is scheduled to answer questions from three US House committees on 1 December.

Market commentators linked the decision to the wider tech sector. Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, argued that the board had little option, since keeping a company this central to the sector without its founder was the greater danger to shareholders. Sam North of eToro said Huang’s comeback showed how heavily the sector’s momentum depends on one person.
items.cav: The sources give different figures for the share and index moves because they measured at different points in trading. The SEC investigation comes from a Reuters report that the BBC did not confirm. Beijing’s denial is the only official response to the espionage allegation in the evidence, and the outcome of the independent investigation is not yet known.
items.op: A reinstatement announced after government assurances, while the investigation is still open, asks shareholders and the public to trust a board that has just reversed itself. The inquiry’s findings should be published in full, not just summarised, before markets and the public treat the matter as closed.

items.t: Next says hackers reached data through a supplier, but customer personal data is not believed compromised
items.s: Clothing and homewares chain Next says hackers reached some of its data via a third-party supplier. It believes customers’ personal details were not exposed, and investigations are still under way.
p: Britain’s high street fashion chain Next has disclosed that an outside technology provider suffered a breach, giving unauthorised people access to some company data. The retailer, which operates more than 800 shops in the UK and Ireland and a further 200 abroad, announced the news on Monday after the provider told it of a “cyber incident”.

The company’s current view is that the compromised material was of minor sensitivity, and that no personal details capable of enabling fraud were taken. According to the Guardian, which cited an understanding rather than a confirmed statement, the files exclude contact information, home addresses, login credentials and bank details.

Next maintains that its own network was untouched, even though the intrusion has reached into the supplier’s environment. In a note to shareholders it described the data as harmless, while stressing that it was handling the case with great care and coordinating with the provider, police and regulators. Those inquiries remain open, so the picture could change.

The BBC’s account differs in emphasis. It reported that only some Next data had been reached, and it placed the company’s headquarters in Enderby, Leicestershire. It also called the supplier an online provider, where the Guardian called it a technology firm. Neither outlet explains what kinds of records were involved.

The episode follows a run of attacks on retail brands. The BBC linked it to October’s breach at the online seller Asos, where an intruder accessed an employee’s account and some customer names and contact details. The Guardian recalled attacks on TFG London, which owns Hobbs and Whistles, in which customer records were accessed, and on Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods last year, which disrupted trading for months. The BBC noted that M&S halted online sales for about six weeks.

Security analyst Alan Simpson of Rapid7 told the Guardian that a breach through a supplier worried him, because attackers tend to target the most loosely guarded entry point. He advised customers to distrust unsolicited messages claiming to come from Next, and to visit the official website or app directly rather than follow links sent to them.
items.cav: The sources differ on scale: the Guardian describes data “relating to” Next, while the BBC says only some of its data was accessed. The claim that customer data was not compromised rests on the company’s present assessment, and the list of excluded data is second-hand, attributed to what is understood rather than confirmed by Next.
items.op: A supplier breach should not be treated as a footnote to a retailer’s reassurances. Customers are entitled to firm, dated answers about which records were taken and why the provider had such broad access. Until Next publishes them, “benign” is a verdict the company has yet to earn.

items.t: Russian navy ship hit by suspected drone attack at Benghazi port, Libyan authorities say
items.s: A Russian navy vessel was reportedly struck by a suspected drone attack at the port of Benghazi in eastern Libya, local authorities said. No one has claimed responsibility, and accounts of casualties and cargo conflict.
p: Libya’s eastern-based government said an explosion at dawn on Sunday aboard a Russian ship docked at Benghazi’s naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack. The ship had stopped to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia under a maritime cooperation agreement, the administration said. Moscow had not commented when the reports were published.

Satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify showed a vessel on fire at the port, and a later image appeared to show the same ship partially submerged. The US-based intelligence firm Vantor said its images identified the ship as the Merkury, a Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette, and showed it mostly capsized and sunk by Sunday. Naval News also identified the ship as the Merkury and said it was almost certainly destroyed.

Officials affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army told the Associated Press that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya. They said at least four drones were intercepted and two hit the warship. These claims come from an initial investigation and have not been independently confirmed.

Casualty reports differ. The eastern government said the site was secured and that there were no casualties. Al Jazeera, citing local sources it did not name, reported an unknown number of Libyan and Russian nationals killed and said the ship was carrying weapons, ammunition and drones. Euronews reported that early accounts had described a fire at an ammunition store before the eastern authorities said the blast came from the ship. None of these details has been verified.

Separately, a sea drone hit a commercial vessel off Benghazi on Sunday evening, according to Reuters military sources. Al Jazeera said the ship was Malta-flagged, and Libya’s health ministry said its injured crew were receiving treatment, some with minor injuries. Counts of intercepted drones also vary: Almasar television said at least 12 were destroyed, while Reuters sources spoke of more than 12 intercepted off the coast.

The eastern government condemned the suspected strike as a violation of Libyan sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety. It said it would pursue legal and diplomatic measures against anyone found responsible and would run a joint investigation with Russia. The Tripoli-based Government of National Unity warned against hosting foreign forces or letting them use facilities, citing “serious fears” about the threat to citizens and national assets.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute, told the BBC he believed Ukraine was behind the attack, though this has not been officially confirmed. He said the Haftar family, which backs the eastern government, was likely to respond. Ukraine has not claimed the strike.

The incident follows a drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday. Finland’s border guard and military said Ukraine was probably responsible. The ship, the Sparta II, had 16 crew members, who were evacuated, and one was slightly injured. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of attacking a tanker in the Mediterranean off Libya.
items.cav: Casualty figures, cargo and the attacker’s identity remain unconfirmed; most attribution comes from anonymous officials or analysts. Drone counts differ between Reuters, Almasar and the AP.
items.op: A foreign warship struck in a port of a state that says it stays out of the war raises the stakes for everyone using that harbour. The public deserves a verified account of who fired, and what the ship carried, from Benghazi, Moscow and Kyiv alike.

items.t: Suspected Ukrainian drone hits Russian warship at Benghazi naval base, Libyan officials say
items.s: A Russian navy corvette was damaged at a naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday. Libyan officials blame a suspected Ukrainian sea drone, in what appears to be the latest incident in the country linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
p: Libyan military officials report that a suspected Ukrainian sea drone struck the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette moored at the Benghazi Naval Base. The blast caused heavy damage to the ship and set off a blaze at the site, the officials said.

Their initial probe, as they describe it, indicates that several sea drones were sent toward the vessel from a facility in western Libya run by Ukrainian forces. Four or more were shot down, while two reached the warship. The officials belong to the self-styled Libyan National Army, which holds the east and south of the country. They gave their account without being named, as they are barred from speaking to the press.

The government based in eastern Libya issued a statement describing an explosion and a fire that crews later brought under control. According to it, the warship had come in for fuel and provisions under a cooperation accord with Russia, though it offered no specifics about the vessel or what it carried. Authorities have opened a joint inquiry with Moscow.

So far nobody has taken credit for the attack, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv had responded by the time of reporting. Later on Sunday, local outlets said a separate sea drone struck a merchant ship off Benghazi, though they supplied no other details. The Almasar satellite broadcaster reported that naval and air units had downed at least 12 more drones near the city.

The rival administration in Tripoli, which the United Nations supports, condemned the risk of “dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts”, which it read as a veiled allusion to the war in Ukraine. It insisted that Libya must not become a arena for foreign states to settle their disputes.

Earlier, in March, Libyan officials said Ukrainian personnel working in the west under a secret arrangement had hit a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean near Malta with a sea drone. Those personnel, largely drone specialists, were based chiefly at an air base in Misrata, with additional presence at military sites in Tripoli and Zawiya, the officials told the Associated Press.
Libya has remained split since the 2011 uprising that ousted Muammar Gaddafi, and its oil resources keep it at the centre of a contest between Russia and the West.
items.cav: Every detail of the strike comes from anonymous Libyan military officials and an eastern government statement. Neither Russia nor Ukraine has commented, and no group has claimed the attack. The drone launch from Ukrainian-run bases in western Libya is unverified, and the reports of a commercial vessel hit and 12 drones destroyed lack further detail.
items.op: Foreign militaries operating on Libyan soil under covert arrangements put ordinary people and ports at risk without any public mandate. Libyans deserve to know which forces are present, on whose authority, and who answers when a strike hits a base. Secret deals that turn a divided country into a battlefield should not survive scrutiny.„}]

items.t: COP31 talks in Turkey close without a deal after fossil fuel row
items.s: Climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, closed without an agreed text after the European Union and other countries rejected a draft that left out fossil fuels. The talks ran past their scheduled end.
p: According to the BBC and Euronews, the COP31 summit in Antalya ended with no consensus on a new agreement. Euronews reported that the negotiations overran by two days, and Al Jazeera described the talks as the longest in the summit's history.

Fossil fuels were the central dispute. The BBC reports that the European Union and several other states turned down a draft that did not refer to phasing them out, which it describes as the largest driver of global climate change. Euronews said an earlier draft had called for an accelerated phase-out, but a later version removed every reference to them. Al Jazeera says oil and gas producers opposed mentioning the fuels at all. The BBC reports that Russia defended that opposition, while an EU representative accused some oil states of hijacking the talks.

Al Jazeera reported that the rejected draft would have, for the first time, acknowledged that global warming is on course to pass 1.5 degrees Celsius, the limit countries had aimed to hold to under the 2015 Paris Agreement. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for helping poorer countries adapt to climate change.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was disappointed by the outcome and blamed powerful fossil fuel interests for obstructing action, according to Al Jazeera. Euronews quoted him saying that those who profit from destroying the planet must not set the terms of the fight against it. Ireland's climate and energy minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the EU would not back a package that omitted fossil fuels, which he called the key driver of climate change.

Other delegations were also critical. Al Jazeera said the Least Developed Countries group, made up of 44 nations representing more than a billion people, struggled to win outcomes for vulnerable states and warned against backsliding. The Marshall Islands said it had been failed by all sides, while Kenya complained that Africa was not specifically named. Saudi Arabia argued that all solutions should stay on the table.

Murat Kurum, Turkiye's environment minister and COP31 president, acknowledged there was no agreement and that the decisions had not been adopted. Al Jazeera reported that he said no new text would be drafted and that existing decisions would be implemented. Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, who led the negotiations, called the outcome disappointing. He pointed to a pledge on electrification signed by more than 90 countries, but said it was not enough on climate action.
Al Jazeera described the collapse as the first such failure since the Copenhagen summit in 2009.
items.cav: The sources give different accounts of the sequence of drafts. The BBC refers to a fourth draft, Al Jazeera to a final draft, and Euronews to a Thursday version and a Sunday text. The sources do not say what implementing existing decisions will involve in practice.
items.op: A summit that cannot name the main cause of warming in its agreed text leaves a gap that no closing statement can fill. Governments that resisted the wording should publicly explain what they were protecting and who gains from it. Transparency about those positions matters more than the headline failure, because it sets the terms for the next round.

items.t: COP31 ends without a major climate deal as fossil fuel and finance disputes divide delegates
items.s: UN climate talks in Turkey failed to produce a major new agreement, after deep disagreements over fossil fuels and money for poorer countries. The conference ran past its scheduled close and became the longest UN climate meeting in history, according to the BBC.
p: Countries failed to reach a major new deal on climate change at the COP31 talks in Turkey, according to the BBC, after divisions over fossil fuels and finance surfaced. Negotiations due to finish on Friday ran late into Sunday in a search for common ground.

The final text was rejected by the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it did not directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming. The words did not appear anywhere in the draft presented in the early hours of Sunday. Its only indirect reference pointed back to a 2023 agreement at COP28 on moving away from them in energy systems.

Irish Minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU, said the bloc “strongly” objected and called a pact without any mention of fossil fuels “unconscionable”. Panama and the Marshall Islands also said the deal did far too little to address the pace of climate change.

Oil-producing states pushed back against stronger language. A draft from Monday that mentioned fossil fuels six times was unacceptable to them. Saudi Arabia’s delegate, Mohammad Ayoub, said Arab countries had continued to engage in good faith and argued that they accounted for only a small share of historical greenhouse gas emissions. Russia warned against “slogans” and claimed that moving away from fossil fuels too quickly would cause fuel poverty.

Finance was the other major sticking point. Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple funding to help poorer countries adapt to heatwaves and droughts. This year’s text contained no concrete figures and no baseline against which that pledge would be measured, raising fears that richer nations would have too much room to manoeuvre. Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa said rich nations and polluting governments “cannot keep arriving empty-handed”.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, attending his last COP before stepping down, said he was “deeply disappointed” and accused “powerful fossil fuel interests” of distorting the science and delaying action. The UK’s Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the lack of a political agreement as “immensely disappointing”, while saying the UK’s commitment was unwavering.

Australia led the official negotiations in a dynamic that some observers described as chaotic. Chris Bowen, Australian minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said there were “unbridgeable red lines” and pointed to what he called the most complicated geopolitical environment in living memory.

The backdrop is stark. The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record, with extreme weather across much of the world. COP31 was also the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how the 1.5C limit agreed in Paris in 2015 would be missed. The last time a COP’s main political agreement collapsed in this way was in Copenhagen in 2009.
items.cav: The account of the talks, including the positions of Saudi Arabia and Russia, relies on the BBC’s reporting and on statements attributed to delegates; the full final text is not quoted. The claim that 2026 could be the hottest year on record is described as a possibility, not a confirmed outcome.
items.op: A climate agreement that cannot name the main cause of the problem is not a compromise worth celebrating. Negotiators should publish finance baselines and emissions language in plain terms, so the public can see who blocked what. Vague pledges without figures let the richest countries avoid accountability.

items.t: Israel opens probe into West Bank arson; opposition leader Eisenkot labels attacks “Jewish terrorism”
items.s: Authorities in Israel are looking into fires set to Palestinian cars and houses in the occupied West Bank. Opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot has described the incidents as “Jewish terrorism.”
p: Officials are examining a set of suspected arson incidents and property damage aimed at Palestinians in the occupied territory. Photographs circulating online showed cars burning and graffiti on walls, one message invoking the biblical name for the West Bank, Judea.

Residents interviewed by news agencies blamed Israeli settlers. Jihad al-Qaq, a local activist, told AFP that a group arrived near the edge of a village at about 2 a.m., torched roughly eight vehicles and sprayed racist messages on homes. Muntasir al-Malik said he was jolted awake by blasts and saw seven cars ablaze. These personal accounts have not been independently verified, and the reports do not identify any suspect.

Israeli troops and police were sent to the affected communities after the reports emerged. The Israel Defense Forces said it “strongly condemns” the conduct. Reporting differs on how widespread the damage was: one broadcaster described attacks across three villages, while DW listed four towns, namely Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashaal, Kafr Malik and Al-Tuwani.

Eisenkot, a rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, posted his condemnation on X and said the blaze amounted to “Jewish terrorism” in every sense. He demanded harsh penalties for those responsible and warned that such sabotage weakens stability in the region and harms Israel’s standing abroad. He is currently involved in talks aimed at forming a new government following the election.

The West Bank has been under Israeli occupation since 1967. Settlements there, which international law considers illegal, are home to more than 500,000 Israelis, while roughly 3 million Palestinians also live in the territory. Attacks on Palestinians have intensified since Hamas’s assault on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the Palestinian Health Ministry says more than 1,100 Palestinians in the West Bank have been killed by Israeli soldiers or settlers.

Eisenkot’s use of the word “terrorists” for violent settlers echoes a description that US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee gave in September. Washington usually applies that label to Palestinian militant groups.
items.cav: The sources do not report any arrests or charges, and no perpetrators are named. The casualty figures come from the Palestinian Health Ministry, and outlets give different counts of affected locations and vehicles.
items.op: Arson against homes and cars is a crime, whoever commits it, and calling it terrorism only matters if investigators identify and prosecute those responsible. Israel’s courts and security services must show that settler violence meets the same consequences as any other attack, or doubts about the rule of law in the West Bank will persist.

items.t: Four West Bank Palestinian villages hit by suspected settler attacks, cars burned and graffiti found
items.s: Overnight attacks that local activists blamed on Israeli settlers left vehicles torched and hostile graffiti in four Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank. Israeli police say they have opened an investigation.
p: On Sunday 22 November 2026, footage from Deir Abu Mashaal, northwest of Ramallah, showed residents looking over burned-out vehicles beside houses daubed with writing. Residents of Kafr Malik, east of the city, faced similar damage and read Hebrew phrases scrawled across walls.

Jihad al-Qaq, a local activist, told AFP that settlers reached the edge of Kafr Malik around 2 am, torched roughly eight cars and left racist notes on homes. Deir as-Sudan and Al-Tuwani were also hit.
Israeli police confirmed an inquiry is underway. The military said it had sent troops and officers to the four villages and denounced the assaults.

The unrest follows a steep escalation in deaths since the Hamas-led assault on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the ensuing Gaza war. An AFP count drawn from Palestinian health ministry data puts at least 1,119 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank over that period. Official Israeli figures record at least 51 Israelis, soldiers among them, killed in Palestinian attacks or clashes in the same span.

Some 500,000-plus settlers share the territory with around three million Palestinians, and international law regards settlements as illegal. The attacks came shortly after new British and Australian sanctions aimed at eight Israeli firms tied to settlement activity.
items.cav: The attacks are only suspected to be by settlers, based on claims from local activists; the sources identify no attackers and report no charges. The casualty tallies come from different sources, and it is unclear whether the military has linked any suspects to the incidents.
items.op: Burning cars and scrawling racist messages on family homes is intimidation, not politics, and it demands swift arrests. Israeli authorities must show that settler violence is pursued as rigorously as any other crime, or the rule of law in the West Bank will remain an empty promise.

items.t: Israeli opposition leader calls settler arson in West Bank ‘Jewish terrorism’
items.s: Overnight arson by Israeli settlers in several Palestinian villages has drawn condemnation from opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and sparked a wider political dispute in Israel. Police say they have opened an investigation.
p: Over the weekend, a large group of settlers moved through Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank, torching roughly a dozen cars and a number of houses and daubing hateful graffiti on walls. According to the Guardian, at least four communities were hit. Israeli police have opened an inquiry and are working with forensic specialists.

Pictures from Kafr Malik, close to Ramallah, showed a Hebrew slogan reading “This is the first revenge.” Vehicles and homes there were set alight. Footage from neighbouring Deir al-Sudan showed cars in flames. Palestinian sources, whose claims the article does not independently verify, said a farm building had burned in Deir Ballut and vehicles had been set on fire in Deir Abu Mashal.

The violence has become a domestic political flashpoint. A recent election produced no clear winner and cost Benjamin Netanyahu his parliamentary majority. Eisenkot has now been tasked with forming a government, a job he has been given 28 days to attempt, with a possible extra fortnight.

Eisenkot called the overnight fires a form of terrorism committed by Jews and said the perpetrators were damaging regional stability and Israel’s security and diplomatic ties. He blamed the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich for pushing the West Bank toward lawlessness, and called on the government and security services to use detention without charge and operations by the Shin Bet internal security agency against those responsible.

Other parliamentarians also turned on Netanyahu. Yair Lapid, who leads Yesh Atid, argued the government had encouraged the attacks, saying ministers were effectively endorsing the violence by staying quiet. Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, warned of a possible third intifada. Noam Tibon, a retired major general and Knesset member, wrote that Israel would be destroyed unless it stopped this kind of violence in the West Bank.

Governments abroad have also responded. Australia imposed sanctions on three individuals and four Israeli entities, one of them a construction firm, over alleged roles in settlement expansion and abuses against Palestinians. The day before, Britain sanctioned eight Israeli construction companies involved in settlement building, which the UN considers occupied Palestinian land under Israeli control since 1967.

The article sets these events against a wider surge in settlement growth and attacks since the Hamas-led assault on Israel on 7 October 2023. It reports that more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces or settlers. It also describes a 72-year-old Palestinian woman shot dead in an overnight settler attack in a village near Jericho, where the group had recently moved into several homes.
items.cav: The article does not say whether any suspects have been identified or arrested, and it gives no casualty figures for the overnight arson. The Palestinian accounts of damage in Deir Ballut and Deir Abu Mashal are unverified. The “Jewish terrorism” label is Eisenkot’s characterisation, not a legal finding.
items.op: Arson against homes and families is a matter of law and order, not partisan rhetoric. Israeli authorities must show that investigations lead to charges and that perpetrators face the same consequences as any other attackers. Ministers who share the settlers’ politics cannot stay silent and still claim to uphold the rule of law.

items.t: COP31 talks in Antalya end without consensus on fossil fuels or climate finance
items.s: Climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya collapsed after almost two days of overtime, with the European Union and Panama rejecting a proposed deal that critics say weakens the shift away from fossil fuels. The summit closed without agreement on phasing out fossil fuels or funding adaptation in poorer countries.
p: After two weeks of difficult negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, which was put forward by the COP presidency. Irish climate minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU on Sunday, said he would not endorse a decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, and described omitting them as “unconscionable.”

Panama also rejected the text, calling it a step backwards and demanding that any decision acknowledge the collective failure to keep warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The Marshall Islands formally objected, saying it would not compromise its future for fossil fuel interests. Australia’s COP31 negotiating president, Chris Bowen, said the breakdown was very disappointing. Russia backed leaving out wording on accelerating a phaseout, arguing that fossil fuels remain a necessary power source. Pakistan and Ghana defended the deal as a necessary compromise.

Finance was another major fault line. Developing states blamed the EU and other wealthy nations for failing to scale up support for adapting to extreme weather. The final text proposed further talks on tripling adaptation finance by 2035 but gave no figure, though it noted that developing countries need some $300 billion a year for adaptation until 2035. Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused rich countries of demanding ambition while withholding money.

Outside the formal process, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels has gained momentum. Tuvalu’s climate minister, Maina Talia, said it was moving towards detailed plans for a global transformation. Several states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have completed or are working on national roadmaps. Brandon Wu of ActionAid USA dismissed such plans as restatements of inadequate policy.

The rejected text recognised electrification as a route to lower emissions and better energy security, and called for raising electricity’s share of final energy demand from about 20 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035. About 75 countries, including China, signed up to that pledge outside the negotiations. It is non-binding and does not say whether the extra power must come from clean sources, which critics say leaves room for fossil fuels.

The talks were the first COP held with the explicit understanding that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, and countries were divided on how to respond to this so-called overshoot. The draft also called for expanding carbon capture and storage to “gigaton scale” by 2035. Scientists see some carbon removal as necessary, but critics say the technology is unproven at scale and expensive. Vanuatu’s climate minister, Ralph Regenvanu, said it had received special attention it did not deserve.

The stakes were heightened by recent disasters, including deadly heatwaves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that the report says killed more than 1,400 people. Geopolitical shocks that pushed oil prices up have also shifted attention towards energy security.
items.cav: The sources give only partial detail on the final draft, and several key claims come from campaigners, ministers or delegations with clear positions. The Nepal death toll is reported without a specified source, and the reasons Russia and others gave for resisting fossil fuel language are presented as their stated arguments, not verified positions.
items.op: A climate summit that will not name the fuel causing the crisis has lost its credibility. Rule-of-law commitments only mean something when they are written down clearly and enforced. Wealthy states should accept binding finance figures and plain language on fossil fuels, or explain openly why they refuse.

items.t: Cop31 talks in Turkey end in division as EU, UK and developing allies reject main climate text
items.s: The UN climate summit in Turkey closed in disarray after the European Union, the United Kingdom and several developing countries rejected the main text, which, according to the Guardian, did not mention fossil fuels. The draft “Antalya pact” will not serve as the summit’s main outcome.
p: The Cop31 talks in Turkey ran past their scheduled Friday close and into Sunday afternoon before the central document collapsed. The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, according to the Guardian. The draft, known as the Antalya pact, was prepared by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the meeting, which gathered close to 200 countries.

Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, spoke on behalf of the EU and said the proposal “failed to meet the moment”. He said the bloc would not endorse a cover decision that did not mention fossil fuels, which he described as the key driver of climate change, and would not accept a decision that greenwashes them. His remarks drew applause in the hall. Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway later raised similar objections.

The pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls on rich countries to provide finance to help poorer nations adapt to climate impacts, and urges countries to minimise the overshoot of the 1.5C threshold set under the Paris agreement. However, it did not endorse the transition away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries had demanded. It also included provisions on carbon capture and storage, which campaigners say perpetuates fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia defended the inclusion of that technology.

The presidencies avoided a complete breakdown by adopting decisions on several related matters, but the cover decision, which was meant to be the main outcome, was not adopted. Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged that there was no agreement on the draft text. He said the presidency had not imposed the text on anyone or issued a take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum, and that it was clear some parties in the hall opposed it.

The Africa group, China and Pakistan did not object to the deal, although the Guardian reports that some of them had reservations. Civil society groups, which have a mandated role at the talks, described the outcome as the worst Cop ever. Mohamed Adow, director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, accused the EU of rejecting the text while bearing responsibility for the crisis, and said European governments were demanding fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding their own fossil fuel output.

Bill Hare, chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics, described the moment as a line in the sand, with countries standing up to fossil fuel interests. The report also places the talks against a year of worsening extreme weather, which it says has claimed tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves and has included a glacier collapse in Nepal, along with droughts and floods made worse by El Niño.

Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and a former UN climate envoy, said there was not enough sense of urgency and criticised the co-presidents for not stepping up to provide leadership as the talks neared their close.
items.cav: The account rests on a single outlet’s reporting. Several claims, including that the text failed to mention fossil fuels and the casualty figures for extreme weather, are presented as reported or attributed rather than independently verified. The Saudi and Africa group positions are given only briefly.
items.op: A summit that cannot name the fuel driving the crisis has failed a basic test of candour. The presidencies owe the public a clear account of who blocked what, and decisions adopted without consensus should be explained openly, not left to procedure. Naming fossil fuels is the minimum that transparency requires.

items.t: COP31 climate talks in Antalya end without a deal as fossil fuel dispute deepens
items.s: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, closed without an agreed declaration after a dispute over whether the final text should name fossil fuels for phaseout. Turkey’s environment minister, who chaired the summit, conceded that the texts had not been approved.
p: Delegates from close to 200 countries converged on Antalya for the UN climate conference, which ran past its scheduled end as negotiators searched for common ground. According to DW, the gathering unfolded against a backdrop of soaring energy prices and tensions linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran, and fossil fuels quickly became the most contentious issue.

In a closing plenary, Murat Kurum, who serves as Turkey’s environment minister and presides over the summit, acknowledged that there was no accord on the text. He said the decisions had therefore not been adopted, which in practice confirmed that no agreement had been reached.

The central disagreement concerned whether the final declaration should call for a phaseout of coal, oil and gas. As DW reports, researchers identify the burning of these fossil fuels as the principal driver of global warming. European governments, smaller island nations and climate campaigners have faulted oil-producing states for leaving the subject out.

Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, who chairs the African Group of Negotiators, faulted the presidency for the way it had managed the talks. He argued that it had failed to show proper regard for the 54 African nations he represents, as well as for his home country, Ghana.

Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told attendees that the negotiations were being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and required an overhaul. He stated that Panama could not back the proposal and warned that the world cannot afford further delay.

Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said the European Union was deeply dissatisfied with the draft under discussion and would not sign off on a text that omitted fossil fuels. Germany’s Environment Minister Carsten Schneider described the latest draft as “not acceptable”.

Former Greenpeace executive Jennifer Morgan argued that ending the summit with no outcome would be preferable to adopting a diluted statement. She faulted the Turkish presidency for poor preparation and for not uniting countries, and said Saudi Arabia’s influence could be seen in the draft. These are Morgan’s own assessments as relayed by DW, and the reporting does not include a reply from the Saudi government.
The conference, originally scheduled to finish on Friday, was prolonged as delegates pursued consensus, but the dispute over fossil fuels has left the talks stuck.
items.cav: The sources describe the positions of several governments and activists, but the reporting does not give a detailed account of the draft text or of the Saudi government’s position. Morgan’s claims about the presidency and Saudi influence are her own views and are not independently confirmed in the evidence.
items.op: A climate summit that cannot name the fuel driving the crisis has failed its basic purpose. Transparency about who blocked the fossil fuel language, and why, is the least delegates owe the countries most exposed to the consequences.

items.t: Six body bags recovered after candy factory fire in Indonesia's Banten province
items.s: Rescuers in Indonesia have retrieved at least six body bags from a candy factory in western Java that was ravaged by fire at the weekend. Police say dozens of staff have not yet been located.
p: According to Indonesian police, the blaze ignited on Saturday at a confectionery plant in Serang Regency, Banten. It began in the late afternoon and was brought under control in the early hours of Sunday.

Police said a combined rescue unit carried the six bags out of the premises. Of the 54 workers listed in company records, 42 had not been accounted for, police added. Eleven had gone home, and one was being treated in hospital.

Senior Superintendent Maruli Ahiles Hutapea told reporters in a written statement that officers were liaising with relatives and the firm to establish who had been in the building when the flames broke out. He said crews would enter the production and office areas only after the structure had cooled and officials certified it as safe.
Footage shared online by Indonesia’s National Search and Rescue Agency, known as Basarnas, showed workers combing through the blackened interior.
The factory operator, Fonusa Agung Mulia, presents itself on its website as a subsidiary of the food group UNIFAM. The sources do not explain what caused the fire.
items.cav: The sources do not say whether the six recovered bodies were employees, and the death toll could rise once the building is searched. Figures on missing staff come from a police statement and have not been independently verified.
items.op: When dozens of workers cannot be traced after a factory fire, the public is owed a clear, regularly updated count. Authorities and the company should disclose how many people were on site and what safety inspections the building passed. Without that openness, families are left waiting in the dark.

items.t: COP31 closes without agreement as EU rejects last-minute text that omits fossil fuels
items.s: The COP31 climate summit ended on Sunday without an agreed deal. The EU presidency said member states objected to an 11th-hour text that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
p: According to the EU presidency, member states objected on Sunday to adopting a late deal that left out explicit references to fossil fuels. The dispute stayed at the centre of the UN climate conference in Antalya, which was held against soaring energy prices and geopolitical tension linked to the war in Iran.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey’s environment minister, acknowledged at the closing plenary that the conference had failed to reach an overarching agreement. “I understand that there is no agreement on this text,” he said, adding that the decisions had therefore not been adopted. He said the text had not been imposed on anyone.

Ireland’s Climate and Energy Minister, Darragh O’Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said the bloc would not endorse a cover decision that fails to name fossil fuels, which he called the key driver of climate change. Any package needed consensus from nearly 200 nations, and negotiators struggled to close the gaps after two weeks of talks.

The EU and other countries had pushed for strong language on moving away from fossil fuels. That push met resistance from Saudi Arabia, which the reporting describes as oil-rich. A draft released earlier in the week called for a faster phase-out, but a shorter version issued on Thursday removed all mentions of coal, oil and gas. Turkey and Australia, the summit co-hosts, convened a hurried meeting between the EU and Saudi Arabia in an effort to find a compromise, and warnings of a walkout were also reported.

The final offer referred to a 2023 global agreement to shift away from fossil fuels but stopped short of naming them. It kept a goal to electrify the global economy, a call to raise the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, and a push to expand carbon capture and storage. Critics of that technology, quoted in the reporting without names, describe it as costly and ineffective at cutting emissions.

French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said in a statement that time was running out and that the group was not yet there. A German official said the situation was difficult and the outcome uncertain, blaming oil-producing countries for a fierce fight. Antigua and Barbuda’s environment minister, Michael Joseph, said he was very disappointed and could not accept the text in its current state, calling the draft quite silent on fossil fuels.

The summit had faced pressure to show progress on rising greenhouse gas emissions, in a year marked by climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal and Indonesia. Turkey and Australia presented electrification, replacing fossil-fuel technologies such as diesel cars and gas heating with electric alternatives, as a way to cut emissions and strengthen energy security.
items.cav: The account rests on a single outlet’s reporting, and the quoted criticism of carbon capture is attributed to unnamed critics. The sources do not say what happens next in the negotiations or whether a revised text will be tabled.
items.op: A climate summit that cannot name the fuel driving the crisis has not earned its consensus. Governments should be willing to say plainly what they are protecting, and negotiators should publish the drafts and the reasons for every deletion. Silence on fossil fuels is not neutral; it is a choice that deserves scrutiny.

items.t: Russian cargo ship still burning in Gulf of Finland after drone strike, Finland says Ukraine likely responsible
items.s: A sanctioned Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad was still on fire on Sunday after a drone attack in the Gulf of Finland, Finnish authorities said. Finland's defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the strike, though Kyiv had not commented.
p: Rescue and firefighting efforts were continuing on Sunday for the Sparta II, a Russian cargo vessel hit by drones on Saturday morning, according to Finnish and Russian officials. The ship was heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad when it was struck, and it later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remains at anchor.

Finland's coastguard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time on Saturday. It said the ship was located roughly 50 km west of the island of Suursaari. Al Jazeera, citing the Finnish Defence Forces, placed the damage in international waters west of Gogland island, so the exact position is described differently across reports.

Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. The Kaliningrad governor, Alexei Besprozvannykh, said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and that there was “no threat” to the territory's supplies. Kyiv has yet to comment publicly.

Water cannon was still being used on Sunday to cool the containers stacked on the deck. Finland said Estonian and Russian vessels were also involved in the recovery work. The Finnish Border Guard said it was not aware of any danger to surrounding shipping and had detected no environmental damage.

Reports differ on the crew. The Finnish Border Guard said the crew had been moved to another Russian vessel, which was already heading back to Russia. Al Jazeera reported that 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship. Earlier, a Russian rescue vessel had been told by the crew that evacuation was not needed.

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo linked the incident to the wider war. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” he said, adding that Ukraine had the right to fight back against the aggressor. Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the Finnish Border Guard was leading the investigation and working with other authorities.

The vessel is subject to sanctions. According to the US government, it was sanctioned in 2022; BBC reporting also says Ukraine sanctioned it earlier this year. Its operator is a Russian company that Al Jazeera identifies as Oboronlogistika, which its website says provides logistics services for Russia's Ministry of Defence.

Estonia's navy commander, Ivo Vark, told ERR that further attacks in the Gulf of Finland could not be ruled out. Finland's military had also said last week that a strike on a Russian warship had taken place in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks. The Baltic Sea has increasingly become a flashpoint since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
items.cav: Attribution to Ukraine comes from Finnish defence forces and is described as likely; Kyiv has not commented, and the sources give no evidence for it. The crew evacuation and the ship's exact location are reported differently, and the drone count is preliminary.
items.op: Blaming Ukraine before an investigation is complete stretches the evidence. Finland should publish what its Border Guard finds, and the sources should separate confirmed facts from claims. When drones and sanctioned cargo move through shared waters, neighbouring states have a stake in transparency, not just in rhetoric.

items.t: Russian drone strike on Kyiv-region apartment block leaves fifteen missing, officials say
items.s: A Russian drone partly destroyed a five-storey apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, and officials have given differing counts of the missing and the dead.
p: Ukrainian police said on Sunday that fifteen people were unaccounted for after a Russian drone destroyed part of an apartment block in Dymer, a settlement north of the capital. Rescue teams were still sifting through debris in the hope of finding survivors. In a post on Telegram, the National Police named two children among those listed as missing: an 11-year-old girl and a seven-year-old boy.

Timur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, gave lower figures. According to one report of his remarks, one body had been pulled from the rubble and three people were hurt. Another report attributed to him said two bodies had been recovered and at least four people injured. He also said a command centre had been created to coordinate the response, with welfare staff and counsellors on site.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said at least fourteen people were missing after the strike, which also injured two others. He described the wider attack as one of the largest of the war so far. Russian forces launched more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles at Ukraine between Thursday night and Friday morning, according to the reports. At least seven people were reported killed in Kyiv, and key bridges over the Dnipro River were damaged.

On Sunday, Zelensky put the week's total at around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles aimed at 20 Ukrainian regions. He said many of the missiles were ballistic, including North Korean models, and accused Moscow of helping Pyongyang improve their accuracy. He called for allies to hurry deliveries of anti-ballistic interceptors, questioned the delays, and urged Washington to approve transfers of interceptors that have already been paid for through NATO’s PURL initiative.

The fighting has also reached the Baltic. Finland warned that the conflict was spreading after a drone set fire to a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic on Saturday. Later that evening, an air alert sounded in Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania, for the first time since the full-scale invasion began. Governor Alexei Bezprozvannykh blamed a suspicious object approaching from Lithuania. The Associated Press could not immediately verify online images said to show drones near Baltiysk, where much of Russia’s Baltic Fleet is based.

Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed its air defences downed 792 Ukrainian drones and four guided bombs in the previous day. It also said Russian troops had seized Sosnovy Bor in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region. Neither claim has been independently confirmed.

In southern Ukraine, Odesa’s education department ordered home learning from November 23 to 27, citing outages of heating, power and water after Russian strikes hit the energy grid. Ukrenergo, the national energy supplier, said conditions in the city and nearby areas were still very hard. Russian media, quoting local authorities, reported five injured in overnight Ukrainian drone attacks on Krasnodar region, four of them in Afipsky.
items.cav: The sources disagree on the Dymer figures: the missing count is given as fourteen and fifteen, the bodies recovered as one and two, and the injured as three and four, all attributed to officials at different points. The Kaliningrad drone claims could not be verified, and the Russian ministry figures and the Krasnodar casualty report are unconfirmed and second-hand.
items.op: When the missing count in a single apartment collapse shifts between officials, the public is left guessing who is still under the rubble. Ukrainian authorities should publish one reconciled tally of the dead, injured and missing in Dymer, and update it openly. Families waiting for news are owed clarity before any other claim.

items.t: Paolo Bulgari, who steered the Bulgari jewellery house into a global luxury brand, dies aged 89
items.s: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari has died in Rome at the age of 89, his family announced. He led the family’s jewellery house for decades and helped turn it into an international luxury name.
p: His relatives honoured him as “the greatest jeweller of our time”, according to Italian media. The Bulgari company also published a tribute on social media, calling him a deeply creative figure whose influence would reach future generations of designers and admirers.

Paolo Bulgari started working with his father in 1960, not long after leaving school, and built a reputation as a specialist in gemstones. He became chairman in 1984 and oversaw the firm’s growth abroad. Together with his brother Nicola and his nephew Francesco Trapani, he pushed the company beyond jewellery and into other categories, including timepieces, fragrances, leather accessories and hospitality.

The house became known for striking coloured stones, heavy gold settings and combinations of colour that broke with convention. Its clients over the years have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn and Marilyn Monroe, as well as more recent names such as Rihanna and Zendaya, and royalty, among them Diana, Princess of Wales.

A major turning point came in 2011, when the Bulgari family handed a controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH in a transaction valued at roughly 3.7 billion euros. According to one account, Paolo Bulgari later called the decision painful, saying it was partly driven by a sense of duty to staff and by worries about handling the transition between generations. He stayed close to the brand and kept designing jewellery in his later years.

Outside the business, he and his wife created the Paolo Bulgari Foundation in 2019 to help young people in disadvantaged districts on the edge of Rome through school and vocational programmes. One of its projects was the redevelopment of a central square in the Tor Bella Monaca district, finished in 2023 with the help of local schools, associations and municipal authorities.
According to the reports, he leaves six children from two marriages. His funeral is scheduled for Monday, 23 November, at the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome.
items.cav: The sources differ on the company’s origins. One says the firm was set up in Rome in the late 19th century by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, who later adapted his name to Bulgari. Another gives the founder as Sotirio Bulgari and the founding year as 1884. The announcement date also varies between the reports, and the family’s statements are reported second-hand through Italian media.
items.op: A family name that becomes a global brand is also a public asset, and the 2011 sale to LVMH shows how quickly such a legacy can pass into a conglomerate’s hands. Transparency about who controls these houses, and on what terms, matters as much as the tributes. Heritage should not excuse opacity.

items.t: Three dead and 36 missing after fire at Indonesian confectionery factory
items.s: A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed at least three people, with 36 others still missing, according to an Indonesian rescue official. Authorities have not yet said what caused the blaze.
p: The fire broke out on Saturday at a factory in Banten province, about 50km west of the capital. Fire crews were alerted at around 4.30pm local time, and when they arrived the building was already engulfed in flames, a fire official told local broadcaster Kompas TV, as cited by The Guardian.

On Sunday, drone footage showed large parts of the complex destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising. Rescuers entered the charred building to search for missing workers, while small fires continued to burn in some spots. The BBC reported that workers were believed to be trapped in parts of the damaged structure.

The Banten governor, Andra Soni, told reporters that an estimated 60 people had been inside the factory when the fire started. Accounts of how many people escaped differ. The national search and rescue agency said 15 survivors had been located, while the Guardian reported that four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and clinic.

According to search and rescue authorities, the factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia.
